about: The right-hand column of the Finds map: biblical people and events from Genesis 1 to Revelation 22, in traditional order. Dates are approximate and follow the traditional reading; where scholars differ, the note says so. Seeded 24 October 2026 by Barnabas.

events.title: Creation
events.note: Archaeology cannot test creation. Babylonian creation stories exist, but they are parallels, not confirmation.

events.title: The Flood
events.note: Several Mesopotamian flood stories survive. No dig has physically confirmed a global flood; the links here are parallels.

events.title: Babel and the nations
events.note: The setting is real: Mesopotamian cities with stepped temple towers (ziggurats), and Ur as a great city. The event itself is untested.

events.title: Abraham, Isaac and Jacob
events.note: No find names Abraham, Isaac or Jacob. Finds show the world Genesis describes was real: Haran, Nahor, and herders moving between Mesopotamia and Canaan.

events.title: Joseph and Israel in Egypt
events.note: No find names Joseph. Semitic people settled in the Nile Delta and served in Egyptian households in this period, which matches the setting.

events.title: Exodus and the wilderness
events.note: Nothing in Egypt directly records the Exodus. Scholars split between an early date (c. 1446 BC, from 1 Kings 6:1) and a late date (c. 1260 BC, from the city name Raamses).

events.title: Conquest and the judges
events.note: By about 1208 BC Egypt knew Israel as a people in Canaan. The destruction layers at Jericho and Hazor are real; their dates and attribution are debated.

events.title: Saul, David and Solomon
events.note: Once doubted as legend, David is named as the founder of a royal house about 150 years after his death. How large his kingdom was is still argued.

events.title: Divided kingdom: Omri, Ahab and Jehu
events.note: From here the kings of Israel appear in their enemies' records by name, and the outside evidence gets dense.

events.title: Assyria and the fall of Samaria
events.note: Assyrian kings recorded tribute from Israel's kings and the deportation of Samaria, as 2 Kings tells it.

events.title: Hezekiah and Sennacherib
events.note: The best documented event in the Old Testament, told from both sides: Judah's in Scripture, Assyria's in stone.

events.title: Josiah to Zedekiah
events.note: Seals and seal impressions name a cluster of the officials Jeremiah names.

events.title: Babylon and the exile
events.note: Babylon's own records note the capture of Jerusalem, the captive king Jehoiachin, and Belshazzar.

events.title: Cyrus and the return
events.note: Persian policy let exiled peoples go home and rebuild their temples. Persian-era papyri name Nehemiah's opponent Sanballat.

events.title: Scripture copied and kept
events.when: c. 600 BC to the 1st century AD
events.note: Not an event in the story; a check on the text itself. Ancient copies show the Scriptures were passed down with great care.

events.title: Herod and the birth of Jesus
events.note: Herod is among the most visible rulers in the archaeological record. The timing of Luke's census under Quirinius is still debated.

events.title: Jesus' ministry in Galilee and Jerusalem
events.note: The towns, synagogues, boats and pools of the Gospels fit what has been dug up, down to small details in John.

events.title: Trial, crucifixion and resurrection
events.note: Archaeology names the men who tried Jesus and shows how Rome crucified. It cannot test the resurrection. That rests on the testimony of eyewitnesses (1 Corinthians 15:3-8), and it is a first-order truth of the faith.

events.title: Acts and Paul's journeys
events.note: Luke uses the right local titles for officials city by city, which matches inscriptions from those cities.

events.title: Fall of Jerusalem, AD 70
events.note: Jesus foretold that the temple would be thrown down. Rome burned the city and carried the temple treasures to Rome.

events.title: Revelation and the seven churches
events.note: The seven cities and the emperor worship they faced are real. Archaeology cannot test the visions themselves.
